lead: A radio voice is thin, clipped and often half lost in noise. The phonetic alphabet, figures said one by one and a few fixed procedure words make sure a name, a berth number or a position arrives exactly as you sent it.

qa.q: How do I spell my yacht's name over the VHF radio?
qa.a: Say the name, then I SPELL, then each letter as its word in the **phonetic alphabet**: "Nova, I SPELL, November Oscar Victor Alfa". Pontoon B is Bravo, never just "B".

blocks.p: On the air B, D, E, P and T all sound alike. So every letter has a word of its own, the same on every ship and in every country. Learn all 26 by heart: you will spell your yacht's name, her call sign, a pontoon letter. Pontoon B is **Bravo**, never just "B".

fig.note: The code flags carry the same names

blocks.cap: A yacht called Nova, spelled out.

blocks.rule: Say the word, then spell it: "Nova, I SPELL, November Oscar Victor Alfa".

qa.q: Why do sailors say "niner" instead of "nine" on the radio?
qa.a: **Niner** cuts through noise, while a plain "nine" is easily taken for "five". Numbers go out figure by figure, so berth 27 is "two seven", and the decimal point is the word "decimal".

blocks.p: Numbers go out figure by figure. "Fifteen" and "fifty" differ by one faint sound, and a yacht ends up at the wrong berth; **one five** and **five zero** cannot be confused. Berth 27 on pontoon D is "pontoon Delta, berth two seven". A nine-figure MMSI is nine separate words, zeros included.

The odd spellings show how to pronounce the figures so that they cut through noise. **Niner** matters most: a plain "nine" is easily taken for "five". The decimal point is the word **decimal**: a draft of 1.9 m is "one decimal niner metres".

qa.q: How do I read out my latitude and longitude on the VHF?
qa.a: **Latitude first**, then longitude, as the plotter shows them: degrees, minutes with "decimal", then north or south, east or west. Longitude always has three figures of degrees, so 24° east begins "zero two four".

blocks.p: Read a position in the order the plotter shows it: **latitude first**, then longitude. Each goes degrees, then minutes with "decimal", then its hemisphere: north or south, east or west. Longitude always has **three figures** of degrees, so 24° east begins "zero two four".

fig.title: Plotter: 38°04.6′N 024°19.5′E
lines: zero four decimal six minutes north,
one niner decimal five minutes east"

blocks.p: Speak at the pace of someone writing it down. A position heard wrong sends help to the wrong place.

sections.title: Who is speaking, and whose turn it is

qa.q: Do I answer RECEIVED or AFFIRMATIVE when the other station asks me a question?
qa.a: **AFFIRMATIVE**, which means yes. RECEIVED only says that the message arrived, and a question still needs its answer: "do you need a diver?" gets AFFIRMATIVE, not RECEIVED.

blocks.p: A VHF channel carries one voice at a time: while you hold the press-to-talk switch you hear nobody. Procedure words, or **prowords**, mark the turns. **THIS IS** stands between the station you call and your own name; leave it out and nobody knows who is calling whom. **OVER** hands the turn across, **OUT** ends the conversation.

fig.note: Pressed: you talk. Released: you listen.

head: Proword
Meaning
rows: I have finished and expect your reply
The call is finished, no reply expected
I heard and understood your message
I need a pause; add the minutes if you can
I did not catch who is calling me

blocks.p: RECEIVED only says that the message arrived. A question still needs its answer: "do you need a diver?" gets AFFIRMATIVE, not RECEIVED. If the caller's name was lost, reply "Station calling Nova, this is Nova, OVER".

blocks.rule: OVER or OUT, never both: you cannot ask for a reply and end the call in one breath.

qa.q: What do I say on the radio if I miss part of a message?
qa.a: **SAY AGAIN**; "repeat" is not used for this on the radio. If only part was lost, ask for that part and name a word you heard: "SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER Delta" gets everything after it.

blocks.p: Sooner or later noise eats part of a message. Ask for it with **SAY AGAIN**; the word "repeat" is not used for this on the radio. If only a part was lost, ask for that part alone and name the word you did hear.

head: You send
You get
rows: Everything after the word you name
Everything before the word you name
The single word that followed it

fig.title: A reply lost in noise
lines: SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER Delta, OVER"
Marina: "I SAY AGAIN, berth two seven"

blocks.p: Your own slip is mended with **CORRECTION**: it cancels what you have just said, and the right version follows. "Berth two three, CORRECTION, berth two five" means berth 25. When you hear it, drop what came before the word and act on what comes after. **I SPELL** warns that the next words are letters of the phonetic alphabet.
